newsitem.title: UK: Britain poised to limit handguns after Dunblane.
newsitem.headline: Britain poised to limit handguns after Dunblane.

text.p: The British government was poised on Tuesday to order a crackdown on the ownership of handguns following an inquiry into the Dunblane massacre in which loner Thomas Hamilton shot dead 16 children and a teacher.

But if, as widely expected, the government merely decided on Wednesday to restrict the weapons to registered gun clubs, it will not satisfy campaigners, backed by the opposition Labour Party, who have called for handguns to be outlawed.
"A complete handgun ban is the only answer to Dunblane," said Ann Pearston, organiser of a petition which has been signed by 750,000 Britons since the tragedy last March.
"Leave handguns in clubs and a planner like Hamilton will just book them out for a competition or put them in his pocket and walk out," she told Labour's annual conference this month.

Prime Minister John Major ordered an inquiry into Dunblane immediately after the tragedy occurred, and has pledged to consider legislation to implement recommendations made by senior Scottish judge Lord Douglas Cullen, who has chaired it.
British newspapers report that Cullen, who handed his report over to the government on Monday, has stopped short of recommending a blanket ban of handgun ownership.

Instead, he is expected to say that people who hold handguns at home should have to move them to a secure gun club. Hamilton, who held firearms certificates issued by the police and was a member of a gun club, used four handguns in the attack.
Hamilton was known locally as a loner with a disturbing fondness for small boys for years before his attack on the gym at Dunblane's primary school, after which he took his own life.

Major called a meeting of senior ministers to discuss the report on Tuesday and Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth is expected to make a statement to parliament on Wednesday setting out its proposals and giving the government's reaction to them.
Forsyth's own parliamentary constituency includes the small Scottish town of Dunblane.

Britain's gun lobby has run a determined campaign to save the sport of shooting, arguing that what is needed to prevent another Dunblane is a tightening up of regulations governing the issue of firearms licences rather than a blanket ban.

"The central (though not the sole) question is: can reforms be made which will help to identify those who should not be allowed to hold firearms, and ensure, in time to prevent tragedy, that they do not have access to firearms," the British Shooting Sports Council said in a statement.
The Council says the vast majority of the 57,000 holders of handgun licences practise target shooting and other legitimate activities, and should not suffer for Hamilton's actions.
These arguments convinced the Conservative majority on parliament's Home Affairs Committee. They issued a report on the massacre in August rejecting calls for handguns to be outlawed.
But the public outcry which greeted their report forced the government to make clear that it was in no way committed to support the views of its own MPs.
Opinion polls show 70 percent of Britons want handguns banned. Labour has vowed to introduce a ban if it wins power at the next election.
Anti-gun campaigners have kept up the pressure, with Pearston saying she may stand against Forsyth at the election unless he accepts her demands.

Lawyers representing parents of the children killed at Dunblane have said they will study Cullen's report to see whether they could sue the police for negligence in not taking away Hamilton's handgun licence.
